source_cards.front: How far from a roadside stop sign, beacon or signal must you park?
source_cards.back: Parking is banned within thirty feet of a stop sign, a flashing beacon or a traffic control signal placed at the roadside.

source_cards.front: How do the four no-parking distances line up?
source_cards.back: The no-parking distances differ by hazard: fifteen feet from a hydrant, twenty feet from a crosswalk at an uncontrolled intersection, thirty feet from a roadside stop sign or signal, and fifty feet from the nearest rail.

source_cards.front: How well must a driver know signs, signals and road markings?
source_cards.back: Every driver must know signs, signals and road markings well enough to recognize them instantly and to obey regulatory signs without hesitating.

source_cards.front: What are the three types of traffic signs?
source_cards.back: Traffic signs fall into three types by function: regulatory, warning, and information or guide signs.

source_cards.front: What do regulatory signs do, what colors are they, and must you obey them?
source_cards.back: Regulatory signs control how traffic moves, are black and white unless shown in their actual color, and must be obeyed.

source_cards.front: What does a YIELD sign tell you to do?
source_cards.back: A YIELD sign tells you to slow down so you can give the right of way to pedestrians crossing and to vehicles on the intersecting road.

source_cards.front: What does a white-on-red regulatory sign about a one-way road or ramp warn?
source_cards.back: A white-on-red regulatory sign warns that you are heading onto a one-way highway or ramp from the wrong direction.

source_cards.front: What does the sign marking a one-way road with oncoming traffic tell you?
source_cards.back: Another regulatory sign marks a one-way roadway whose traffic is coming toward you, and you may not enter it at that point.

source_cards.front: What does the railroad regulatory sign tell you to do?
source_cards.back: The railroad regulatory sign means approach with caution and make sure every track is clear before you cross.

source_cards.front: What does a no-left-turn sign mean?
source_cards.back: A no-left-turn sign means you may not turn left at that intersection.

source_cards.front: May you park under a no-parking sign if you stay in the car?
source_cards.back: Under a no-parking sign you may not park in the area even if you remain inside the car.

source_cards.front: When does a school-zone speed limit apply?
source_cards.back: A school-zone speed limit applies during the hours the sign shows, and it may also be displayed on a lighted sign with flashing amber lights.

source_cards.front: What does a LEFT LANE MUST TURN LEFT sign mean?
source_cards.back: A LEFT LANE MUST TURN LEFT sign means traffic in the left lane has to turn left at the intersection ahead.

source_cards.front: What does a NO TURNS sign mean?
source_cards.back: A NO TURNS sign means you may turn neither right nor left at that intersection.

source_cards.front: What does one regulatory sign mark about passing?
source_cards.back: One regulatory sign marks where a no-passing zone begins.

source_cards.front: What does the regulatory sign telling you not to drive to its left require?
source_cards.back: One regulatory sign tells you not to drive to the left of it.

source_cards.front: What does a one-way arrow sign mean?
source_cards.back: A one-way arrow sign means you may travel only in the direction the arrow points.

source_cards.front: What colors are warning signs and construction warning signs?
source_cards.back: Warning signs are black on yellow, except construction-area warning signs, which are black on orange, and they warn of hazards that call for extra caution.

source_cards.front: What does fluorescent yellow on a sign mark?
source_cards.back: Fluorescent yellow on a sign marks pedestrian crossings and school zones.

source_cards.front: What shape are most warning signs?
source_cards.back: Most warning signs are diamond shaped, though there are some exceptions.

source_cards.front: How do the three warning color schemes differ?
source_cards.back: Ordinary warning signs are black on yellow, construction warning signs are black on orange, and fluorescent yellow is kept for pedestrian crossings and school zones.

source_cards.front: What do curve warning signs tell you?
source_cards.back: Curve warning signs tell you of a sharp left turn, a curve to the right, a gradual curve right then left, or a winding road ahead.

source_cards.front: What do side-road warning signs show?
source_cards.back: Side-road warning signs show that a side road joins the highway ahead, either from the right or at an angle.

source_cards.front: What does a BUMP sign tell you?
source_cards.back: A BUMP sign warns of a bump ahead and tells you to slow down.

source_cards.front: What does the warning sign for a road that does not continue straight mean?
source_cards.back: One warning sign means the road does not continue straight, so you must turn right or left.

source_cards.front: What does a SOFT SHOULDER sign warn?
source_cards.back: A SOFT SHOULDER sign warns that the roadside is soft, so stay on the pavement.

source_cards.front: What do the warnings for reverse sharp turns and a road ending both ways show?
source_cards.back: Other warning signs show a sharp left turn followed by a sharp right, or a road that ends ahead and turns both right and left.

source_cards.front: What do arrow signs for sharp turns warn, and how are they set up?
source_cards.back: Arrow signs warn of a sharp turn or curve in the direction of the arrow and are normally set up in a series.

source_cards.front: What do ROAD NARROWS and PAVEMENT NARROWS signs mean?
source_cards.back: A ROAD NARROWS sign means the road ahead is narrower than the one you are on, and a PAVEMENT NARROWS sign means the paved surface ahead is narrower.

source_cards.front: What does an island-ahead warning sign allow?
source_cards.back: An island-ahead warning sign means you may pass the island on either side.

source_cards.front: What does a DIP sign tell you?
source_cards.back: A DIP sign warns of a dip in the road and tells you to slow down.

source_cards.front: What does a ONE LANE BRIDGE sign mean?
source_cards.back: A ONE LANE BRIDGE sign means the bridge ahead has no room for you to meet or pass another car or truck.

source_cards.front: What do STOP AHEAD and YIELD AHEAD signs warn?
source_cards.back: STOP AHEAD and YIELD AHEAD signs warn that a STOP sign or a YIELD sign is coming up.

source_cards.front: Where does the stop or yield actually happen after a STOP AHEAD or YIELD AHEAD sign?
source_cards.back: STOP AHEAD and YIELD AHEAD signs only warn that a control is coming; the stop or yield itself happens at the STOP or YIELD sign further on.

source_cards.front: What does a railroad-crossing-ahead warning sign tell you to do?
source_cards.back: A railroad-crossing-ahead warning sign means slow down, look carefully both ways and be ready to stop, since a train cannot stop quickly.

source_cards.front: What does a low-shoulder sign warn?
source_cards.back: A low-shoulder sign warns that the shoulder sits much lower than the road surface.

source_cards.front: What do truck-crossing and fire-station signs tell you?
source_cards.back: Truck-crossing and fire-station signs tell you to watch for trucks or fire trucks pulling onto the road.

source_cards.front: What do PAVEMENT ENDS and DEAD END signs mean?
source_cards.back: A PAVEMENT ENDS sign warns that the surface ahead turns to gravel or dirt, and a DEAD END sign means the street has no outlet.

source_cards.front: What do lane-ends signs warn, and why come three in a series?
source_cards.back: Lane-ends signs warn that the number of lanes changes ahead, and the three signs come in a series as a repeated reminder to merge into the next lane.

source_cards.front: Where does the NO PASSING ZONE warning sign stand?
source_cards.back: The NO PASSING ZONE warning sign stands on the left side of a two-lane road to warn where a no-passing zone begins.

source_cards.front: Which side of a two-lane road should you look for the no-passing warning sign?
source_cards.back: The no-passing warning sign belongs on the left side of a two-lane road, at the point where the zone begins, so look left for it.

source_cards.front: What does a low-clearance sign mean?
source_cards.back: A low-clearance sign means vehicles or loads taller than the clearance shown cannot fit under the structure ahead.

source_cards.front: What does a two-way traffic sign tell you?
source_cards.back: A two-way traffic sign means you are leaving a separated one-way roadway for a two-way road, and it also reminds drivers they are on a two-way road.

source_cards.front: Which road changes do other warning signs announce?
source_cards.back: Other warning signs announce a traffic signal ahead, a crossroad, a divided highway starting or ending, and a downhill grade.

source_cards.front: Which hazards do other warning signs flag?
source_cards.back: Warning signs also flag slippery-when-wet pavement, a narrow bridge, cattle crossings and deer crossings.

source_cards.front: What does a pedestrian-crossing sign mean, and what must you do?
source_cards.back: A pedestrian-crossing sign marks a spot where people on foot often cross, not always at an intersection, and you must yield to pedestrians in the crosswalk while watching both sides.

source_cards.front: What do school-crossing and school bus stop signs tell you?
source_cards.back: A school-crossing sign means slow down and watch for children crossing, and a separate sign warns of a school bus stop ahead.

source_cards.front: What does one bicycle sign state about passing a cyclist?
source_cards.back: One bicycle sign states that a three foot minimum clearance is required when passing a cyclist.

source_cards.front: What does another bicycle sign tell drivers about a narrow lane?
source_cards.back: Another sign tells drivers that a cyclist may use the full lane when the travel lane is narrow.

source_cards.front: What does a ROAD CONSTRUCTION sign mean for you?
source_cards.back: A ROAD CONSTRUCTION sign means you are entering a work area, so watch for a flagman, one-way traffic, other signs or obstructions, go carefully and follow instructions.

source_cards.front: What other work-zone hazards do signs warn of?
source_cards.back: Work-zone signs also warn of a flagman ahead, workers in or near the road, and mowing equipment ahead.

source_cards.front: What does the crossbuck sign mean, and what does a sign beneath it show?

source_cards.front: When do statutory speed limits apply?
source_cards.back: Statutory limits apply unless a different speed zone has been set and posted on official regulatory signs.

source_cards.front: Where exactly do you stop at a STOP sign?
source_cards.back: At a STOP sign, stop at the marked line; with no line, before the near crosswalk; with neither, at the point nearest the cross street where you can see traffic.

source_cards.front: What must any turn on red do, and where is it banned?
source_cards.back: Any turn on red must yield to traffic and pedestrians lawfully in the intersection and is not allowed where a sign prohibits it.

source_cards.front: What does a flashing red signal mean?
source_cards.back: A flashing red signal means the same as a STOP sign.

source_cards.front: Which other places and people require you to stop?

source_cards.front: What must you do at a YIELD sign facing you?
source_cards.back: At a YIELD sign facing you, slow down and stop if needed for vehicles and pedestrians lawfully crossing.

source_cards.front: What must you do at a steady red light, and which turns may follow a stop?
source_cards.back: At a steady circular red light, stop and stay stopped until it turns green, although a right turn, and in certain cases a left turn, is allowed after stopping.

source_cards.front: What must you do when red lights flash at a railroad crossbuck?
source_cards.back: Red flashing lights work with crossbuck signs at many railroad crossings, and you must always stop when they begin flashing because a train is near, checking every track before you cross.

source_cards.front: When gates are used with flashing lights, when do you stop and how long do you wait?
source_cards.back: Where gates are used with flashing lights, stop as soon as the lights start, before the gates come down, and stay stopped until the gates rise and the lights stop.

source_cards.front: What do turn arrows control?
source_cards.back: Arrows control specific turning movements, and yellow and green arrows give left turns the same control that the standard light gives through traffic.

source_cards.front: What does a green arrow let you do?
source_cards.back: A green arrow lets you go in the arrow's direction while opposing traffic has to stop.

source_cards.front: What does a steady green arrow with other lights allow?
source_cards.back: A steady green arrow, alone or with other lights, lets you enter for the arrow's movement or any other movement the other lights allow, still yielding to pedestrians and vehicles lawfully in the intersection.

source_cards.front: What does a yellow arrow after a green arrow mean?
source_cards.back: Yellow arrows follow green arrows to show the protected movement is ending, and a steady yellow arrow shown with a circular green means that protected turn is ending.

source_cards.front: What does a steady yellow arrow alone or with red mean?
source_cards.back: A steady yellow arrow shown alone or with a steady circular red clears the protected turn, and you may not enter the intersection after it goes out.

source_cards.front: How does a green arrow differ from a yellow arrow?
source_cards.back: A green arrow is a protected turn with opposing traffic stopped, and a yellow arrow means that protection is ending.

source_cards.front: What does a steady green arrow over a lane mean?
source_cards.back: A steady green arrow over a lane means you may drive in that lane while obeying all other controls and normal safe practice.

source_cards.front: How do the red X, green arrow and yellow X over a lane differ?
source_cards.back: Over a lane, a red X closes it, a green arrow opens it, and a yellow X allows it only with caution.

source_cards.front: What is a roundabout, and which way does traffic travel?
source_cards.back: A roundabout is a circular intersection, usually without a traffic signal, where traffic travels counter-clockwise around a central island.

source_cards.front: What may you do at a red light after stopping?
source_cards.back: At a red light, wait for green and a clear way, though you may turn right after stopping if you are in the proper lane.

source_cards.front: How do you treat an intersection with a dead traffic light?
source_cards.back: Treat an intersection with a dead traffic light as a four-way stop.

source_cards.front: What does a flashing red signal mean?
source_cards.back: A flashing red signal means the same as a STOP sign.

source_cards.front: What must you do when following or meeting a stopped school or church bus with its arm out?
source_cards.back: Following or meeting a stopped school or church bus with its stop arm out and red lights flashing, stop and stay stopped until the arm folds and lights go off.

source_cards.front: What do red flashing lights and the stop arm mean, and how far back do you stop?
source_cards.back: Red flashing lights with the stop arm out mean the bus is loading or unloading, and drivers from either direction stop at least twenty feet from it.

source_cards.front: How do amber and red school bus lights differ?
source_cards.back: Amber bus lights mean get ready, with red lights and stop arm meaning stop at least twenty feet away.

source_cards.front: Must drivers on a green arrow still yield?

source_cards.front: What markings does a load reaching four feet or more past the rear need?
source_cards.back: A load reaching four feet or more past the rear needs a red flag at least twelve inches square by day and a red light visible for two hundred feet at night.

source_cards.front: What does the move-over law require on four or more lanes?
source_cards.back: On roads of four or more lanes, leave the lane next to a stopped emergency vehicle with flashing lights or a wrecker with amber lights.

source_cards.front: What are the four general types of pavement markings?
source_cards.back: Pavement markings generally come in four types: centerline striping, edge striping, crosswalks and pavement messages.

source_cards.front: What does a solid yellow line beside a broken line mean for you?
source_cards.back: Where passing is restricted, a solid yellow line runs beside the broken line, and if the solid line is on your side you may not pass.

source_cards.front: What do two solid yellow lines mean?
source_cards.back: When passing is banned for traffic in both directions, the broken line is replaced by two solid yellow lines.

source_cards.front: How do a broken line, one solid line on your side and two solid lines differ for passing?
source_cards.back: A solid yellow line on your side bans your passing, two solid yellow lines ban passing both ways, and a broken line alone allows passing when safe.

source_cards.front: What separates lanes moving the same way, and may you cross those lines?
source_cards.back: Two or more lanes moving the same way are separated by broken white lines, and you may cross them when passing.

source_cards.front: What does a normal solid white line between same-direction lanes mean?
source_cards.back: A normal solid white line separates lanes going the same direction where crossing is discouraged but not forbidden.

source_cards.front: What does a wide solid white line add?
source_cards.back: A wide solid white line adds emphasis where crossing calls for unusual care.

source_cards.front: What does a double solid white line between same-direction lanes mean?
source_cards.back: A double solid white line separates lanes going the same direction, and crossing it is prohibited.

source_cards.front: Where do crosswalk lines appear, and when must you stop at one?
source_cards.back: Solid white lines mark crosswalks at intersections and sometimes between them, and with no controlling signal a driver must stop at any crosswalk occupied by pedestrians.

source_cards.front: Which lane do you use in a two-lane roundabout for each move?
source_cards.back: In a two-lane roundabout, use the right lane for right turns and the left lane for left turns and U-turns, and to go straight follow the pavement markings, arrows or signs.

source_cards.front: When should you expect a train, and what should you do in heavy traffic?

source_cards.front: What should you watch for after the last car of a train passes?

source_cards.back: For a right turn from a four-lane or divided highway, get into the right lane well ahead and turn tightly into the right lane of the cross street.

source_cards.front: How do you make a left turn from a four-lane or divided highway?
source_cards.back: For a left turn there, move to the lane nearest the center line or divider, turn from the inside lane without a wide swing, and enter just right of the cross street's center line, unless signs or markings allow turns from more lanes.

source_cards.front: How does lane choice differ for right and left turns from a four-lane highway?
source_cards.back: A right turn from a four-lane highway starts in the right lane and ends tight in the cross street's right lane, while a left turn starts from the inside lane nearest the center line.

source_cards.front: When is a three-point turn normally allowed?
source_cards.back: A three-point turn reverses your direction and must not endanger other traffic, so it is normally allowed only where you can be seen from far away and traffic makes it safe.

source_cards.front: Where are three-point turns banned?
source_cards.back: Three-point turns are banned on interstate freeways, on curves, and near hilltops where drivers approaching within five hundred feet from either direction cannot see you.

source_cards.front: Who governs three-point turns, and will there always be a sign?
source_cards.back: Local ordinances govern three-point turns, there may be no warning signs, and prohibiting signs are usually posted only at hazardous spots.

source_cards.front: Can a three-point turn be prohibited where no sign forbids it?
source_cards.back: Three-point turns are prohibited where oncoming drivers within five hundred feet cannot see you, even when no sign forbids the turn.

source_cards.front: Where does a cyclist ride on a roadway, and when may the rider move left?
source_cards.back: A cyclist on a roadway rides as close as practicable to the right curb or edge, except when passing, preparing a left turn, or avoiding hazards such as debris, opening car doors or pedestrians.

source_cards.front: How can cyclists keep right yet still ride two abreast or move left?
source_cards.back: Cyclists normally keep as far right as practicable, yet they may also ride two abreast at all times and move left to pass, to turn left, or to avoid hazards.

source_cards.front: What should you do before turning left in front of an oncoming motorcycle?
source_cards.back: Left turns in front of an oncoming motorcycle cause a large share of car-motorcycle injury crashes, so look twice and know the motorcycle's speed before you turn left.

source_cards.front: Why is seeing a motorcycle not enough before a left turn?
source_cards.back: Seeing a motorcycle is not enough before a left turn, because drivers also misjudge its distance and speed, so look again and know its speed first.

source_cards.front: What is an interchange?
source_cards.back: An interchange joins two highways at different levels with separate connecting roads, so vehicles can cross, enter or leave without interfering with others.

source_cards.front: What are the four common interchange types?

source_cards.front: What does a directional interchange serve?
source_cards.back: A directional interchange serves heavy traffic moving between only two legs, with other movements handled by ordinary diamond-type ramps.

source_cards.front: What does a cloverleaf interchange use, and what does it remove?
source_cards.back: A cloverleaf interchange uses loop connections for turns on and off the freeway from four directions and removes left-turn and cross-traffic conflicts.

source_cards.front: How does a diamond interchange work?
source_cards.back: A diamond interchange has four ramps for entering or leaving with the flow, and left turns are made after you leave the freeway.

source_cards.front: When is a trumpet interchange used?

source_cards.front: Where do left turns happen at a diamond interchange?
source_cards.back: A diamond interchange lets you enter and leave with the flow on four ramps, and any left turn comes only after you are off the freeway, never on it.

source_cards.back: You enter a roundabout from the right, yielding to vehicles already circulating, and follow the circle to the right until you reach your road.

source_cards.front: Why are roundabouts spreading in the United States?
source_cards.back: Roundabouts are spreading in the U.S. because one-way counterclockwise flow creates fewer conflict points and moves traffic more safely and efficiently than standard intersections.

source_cards.front: How much do roundabouts cut crashes compared with other controls?
source_cards.back: Compared with other intersection controls, roundabouts cut fatal crashes about ninety percent, injury crashes about seventy-five percent and all crashes about thirty-five percent, according to the crash statistics the manual cites.

source_cards.front: What should you do before entering a roundabout?
source_cards.back: To drive a roundabout, slow down, obey the signs, and yield to pedestrians and bicyclists before you enter.

source_cards.front: Whom must you yield to when entering a roundabout?
source_cards.back: Yield to traffic coming from your left that is already in the roundabout, and enter only when there is a safe gap.

source_cards.front: How fast should you go inside a roundabout, and how do you leave?
source_cards.back: Keep your speed low inside the roundabout and turn off onto your road as you reach its exit.

source_cards.front: Which way do pedestrians look at a roundabout crosswalk?
source_cards.back: At a roundabout, pedestrians at the curb look left for oncoming traffic, while those on the crosswalk island look right.

source_cards.front: How may bicyclists use a roundabout?
source_cards.back: Bicyclists may ride through the roundabout or use the crosswalk instead.

source_cards.front: Who has the right-of-way at a roundabout?
source_cards.back: Vehicles already in a roundabout have the right-of-way.

source_cards.front: May you turn left to enter a roundabout?
source_cards.back: Never turn left to enter a roundabout; wait for a safe gap and turn right into it.

source_cards.front: Whom must you yield to as you leave a roundabout?
source_cards.back: Yield to pedestrians and bicycles as you leave the roundabout.

source_cards.front: What should you do if you miss your exit in a roundabout?
source_cards.back: If you miss your exit, go around the roundabout again, and never back up inside it.

source_cards.front: What do you do for an emergency vehicle at a roundabout?
source_cards.back: For an emergency vehicle, pull over before entering if you are not yet in the roundabout; if you are already in, continue to your exit and then pull over, avoiding any stop inside.

source_cards.front: How does the response to an emergency vehicle differ before and after entering a roundabout?
source_cards.back: An emergency vehicle means pull over if you have not entered the roundabout, but keep going to your exit first if you are already inside.

source_cards.front: What is a truck apron, and who uses it?
source_cards.back: A truck apron is a paved area on the inside of a roundabout for the rear wheels of large trucks, and cars, pickups and SUVs are not meant to use it.

source_cards.front: When may you stop inside a roundabout?
source_cards.back: Once inside a roundabout, do not stop unless stopping is the only way to avoid a crash or other danger.

source_cards.front: What must you do before entering a two-lane roundabout?
source_cards.back: In a two-lane roundabout, pick your lane and yield to traffic in both lanes before you enter.

source_cards.front: Which lane do you use in a two-lane roundabout for each move?
source_cards.back: In a two-lane roundabout, use the right lane for right turns and the left lane for left turns and U-turns, and to go straight follow the pavement markings, arrows or signs.

source_cards.front: What is double parking, and is it allowed?

source_cards.front: What road rights and duties do people on bicycles have?
source_cards.back: People on bicycles have the same road rights and responsibilities as people in motor vehicles, so drivers and cyclists alike must know and obey state traffic laws.

source_cards.front: Where does a cyclist ride on a roadway, and when may the rider move left?
source_cards.back: A cyclist on a roadway rides as close as practicable to the right curb or edge, except when passing, preparing a left turn, or avoiding hazards such as debris, opening car doors or pedestrians.

source_cards.back: People on bicycles may ride two abreast at all times, and they must ride with the flow of traffic.

source_cards.front: How can cyclists keep right yet still ride two abreast or move left?
source_cards.back: Cyclists normally keep as far right as practicable, yet they may also ride two abreast at all times and move left to pass, to turn left, or to avoid hazards.

source_cards.front: How do cyclists signal turns, lane changes and stops?
source_cards.back: Cyclists signal turns, lane changes and stops with the same hand and arm signals that drivers use.

source_cards.front: Where must cyclists ride when there is a bicycle lane, and may they use sidewalks?
source_cards.back: Cyclists must use a bicycle lane where one exists; sidewalks and multipurpose paths are not bicycle lanes, and riding a bicycle on the sidewalk is illegal in Alabama.

source_cards.front: Which cyclists must wear helmets, and where?
source_cards.back: Cyclists under sixteen must wear a securely fastened helmet on public roads, other public rights-of-way, public bicycle paths and in public parks.

source_cards.front: When may a driver enter a bicycle lane?
source_cards.back: A driver may enter a bicycle lane only to park where parking is allowed, to enter or leave the highway, or to prepare for a turn.

source_cards.front: How do you turn across a bicycle lane?
source_cards.back: To turn across a bicycle lane, move into the lane before the turn, but only when doing so does not endanger a cyclist using it.

source_cards.front: What are a driver's only reasons to use a bicycle lane, and how is a turn across it made?
source_cards.back: Drivers stay out of bicycle lanes except to park, enter or leave the highway, or prepare a turn, and for a turn across the lane they move into it first when it is safe.

source_cards.front: How much room must you leave when passing a cyclist, and why?
source_cards.back: Alabama law requires at least three feet between your vehicle and a person on a bicycle when you pass, and wind from fast vehicles can push a cyclist enough to cause a crash.

source_cards.front: Who does the helmet rule cover compared with the passing clearance rule?
source_cards.back: The bicycle helmet rule applies to riders under sixteen, while the three-foot passing clearance applies to every driver passing any cyclist.

source_cards.front: Where should you avoid passing a cyclist?
source_cards.back: Avoid passing a cyclist uphill, on curves, where visibility is limited, or when other vehicles occupy the lane you would need to use.

source_cards.front: What should you do when a narrow road makes passing a cyclist unsafe?
source_cards.back: When a narrow road makes passing unsafe, stay a safe distance behind the cyclist, without tailgating or blasting the horn, until you can pass.

source_cards.front: Where should you watch most closely for cyclists?
source_cards.back: Watch closely for cyclists at intersections, when crossing sidewalks, and when entering or leaving alleys or driveways.

source_cards.front: How does wet weather affect a bicycle's braking?
source_cards.back: A bicycle brakes far less well in wet weather, so drivers should allow for its reduced ability to slow or stop.

source_cards.front: What should bicycles carry at night, and what should drivers do?
source_cards.back: State law says bicycles should carry lights or reflectors for night riding, and drivers need extra caution in darkness or poor visibility.

source_cards.front: What causes most rear-end collisions, and which space can you control most easily?
source_cards.back: Following too closely causes most rear-end collisions, and the space ahead of your car, called following distance, is the space you can control most easily.

source_cards.front: What should decide your following distance?
source_cards.back: Set your following distance by the speed of traffic and the condition of the road, leaving enough room to stop if you must.

source_cards.front: Which rule replaced one car length for every ten miles per hour?
source_cards.back: The old rule of one car length for every ten miles per hour has given way to the two-second rule, which the manual calls easier to apply and safer.

source_cards.front: How do you use the two-second rule?
source_cards.back: For the two-second rule, pick a fixed object ahead, start counting one thousand one, one thousand two as the car ahead passes it, and if you reach it first, ease off until the gap is safe.

source_cards.front: What first decides actual stopping distance, and what does stopping distance help decide?
source_cards.back: How far your car needs to stop helps decide a safe speed, and actual stopping distance depends first on the driver's mental and physical reaction time.

source_cards.front: How does pavement affect stopping distance?
source_cards.back: Pavement type and condition change stopping distance a great deal, since rough dry concrete grips far better than slippery brick or smooth asphalt.

source_cards.front: What does the stopping chart show at twenty-five miles per hour?
source_cards.back: The manual's stopping-distance chart gives twenty-seven feet of thinking distance plus thirty-four point seven feet of braking distance, or sixty-one point seven feet in total, at twenty-five miles per hour

source_cards.front: What does the stopping chart show at sixty-five miles per hour?
source_cards.back: At sixty-five miles per hour the chart shows seventy-one feet of thinking distance and two hundred thirty-four point seven feet of braking distance, a total of three hundred five point seven feet.

source_cards.front: What happens in a skid?
source_cards.back: A skid happens when the tires lose their grip, and then the engine, brakes and even steering lose effect.

source_cards.front: Should you brake during a skid?
source_cards.back: Do not brake in a skid until you regain your forward direction, since braking speeds the skid and locked front wheels lose steering.

source_cards.front: How do you recover from a skid in a rear-wheel drive car?
source_cards.back: To end a skid, keep the rear from outrunning the front; in a rear-wheel drive car, easing off the gas slows the rear wheels and, with steering, straightens the car.

source_cards.front: How do you recover from a skid in a front-wheel drive car?
source_cards.back: In a front-wheel drive car, a light touch on the gas speeds the front wheels so the front catches up and the skid straightens.

source_cards.front: What is the next best step if there is no room to accelerate in a skid?
source_cards.back: Without room to accelerate, the next best step is to disengage the transmission and steer the way the rear is skidding, though many experts warn against shifting to neutral in a panic.

source_cards.front: At what speeds does hydroplaning start and become total in a standard car?
source_cards.back: On wet roads most tires wipe the surface up to thirty-five miles per hour, but in a standard car partial hydroplaning starts near thirty-five miles per hour and can become total near fifty-five miles per hour

source_cards.front: What happens during total hydroplaning?
source_cards.back: With total hydroplaning there is no friction to brake, speed up or turn, so wind or a slight curve can cause an uncontrollable skid.

source_cards.front: What should you do if you hydroplane?
source_cards.back: If you hydroplane, take your foot off the accelerator; correct a partial-hydroplane skid, but in a total one just release the gas and ride it out.

source_cards.front: How do tires affect hydroplaning, and when is complete hydroplaning expected?
source_cards.back: Good tires with deep tread help prevent hydroplaning, but when water is deeper than the tread, expect complete hydroplaning above fifty miles per hour

source_cards.front: What is the basic rule in any driving emergency?
source_cards.back: In any emergency, think before you act, since instinct, like slamming the brakes in a skid, can be the wrong move.

source_cards.front: What can you do if pumping the brakes does not work?
source_cards.back: If pumping fails, apply the parking brake gently to avoid a skid, shift to a lower gear, or switch off the engine in gear, knowing power steering and brakes then stop assisting.

source_cards.front: What does it mean not to overdrive your headlights?
source_cards.back: Never overdrive your headlights: keep a speed at which you can stop within the distance your lights show ahead.

source_cards.front: How far do high beams usually light the road?
source_cards.back: Under normal conditions, high beams usually light the road about three hundred fifty feet ahead.

source_cards.front: How close to other vehicles must you dim your headlights?
source_cards.back: The law requires dimming your headlights within five hundred feet of an oncoming vehicle and within two hundred feet of a vehicle you are following.

source_cards.front: What if an oncoming driver keeps high beams on after you dim?
source_cards.back: If an oncoming driver keeps high beams on after you dim, keep yours dimmed anyway, since blinding that driver only endangers you.

source_cards.front: When does state law require headlights?
source_cards.back: State law requires headlights, not just parking lights, starting a half-hour after sunset and lasting until a half-hour before sunrise, and also whenever you cannot see clearly for at least five hundred feet.

source_cards.front: What should you do if you are unsure whether lights are needed?
source_cards.back: When unsure whether lights are needed, turn them on low beam, which helps you see and helps others see you.

source_cards.front: How do the dimming distances compare with the visibility distance for headlights?
source_cards.back: Dim within five hundred feet of oncoming traffic and within two hundred feet behind a car, while headlights are required whenever you cannot see five hundred feet ahead.

source_cards.front: Why is speed more dangerous at night?
source_cards.back: Speed is more dangerous at night because at high speed your headlight range does not give enough stopping distance, so obey limits even on roads you know.

source_cards.front: When does Alabama law require headlights with wipers?
source_cards.back: Alabama law requires headlights whenever wipers are running for rain, sleet or snow, but intermittent wiper use does not require them.

source_cards.front: How should you drive in fog or a snowstorm?
source_cards.back: Avoid driving in fog or a snowstorm unless absolutely necessary, and when visibility is limited, slow down enough to stop within the distance you can see.

source_cards.front: Which beams should you use in fog or heavy snow?
source_cards.back: Use low beams in fog or heavy snow to cut the glare thrown back at you.

source_cards.front: What should you do if your headlights fail?
source_cards.back: If headlights fail, try the parking lights and turn signals; on a dark empty road, slow down on the pavement before moving onto the shoulder.

source_cards.front: How far must lights be visible, and how far must high beams reach?
source_cards.back: All lights must be visible from at least five hundred feet, and the high beam must light objects at least three hundred fifty feet away and stay properly aimed.

source_cards.back: Rear view mirrors must show two hundred feet behind, while every light must be visible from five hundred feet and high beams must reach three hundred fifty feet.

source_cards.front: What vehicles need a Class A license?
source_cards.back: Class A is for combination vehicles with a combined weight rating over twenty-six thousand pounds when the towed vehicle is rated over ten thousand pounds.

source_cards.front: What vehicles need Class B and Class C licenses?
source_cards.back: Class B is for single vehicles rated over twenty-six thousand pounds towing no more than ten thousand pounds, and Class C is for vehicles built for sixteen or more people including the driver or placarded for hazardous materials.

source_cards.front: What separates Class A from Class B when both involve heavy vehicles?
source_cards.back: Class A and Class B both involve vehicles rated over twenty-six thousand pounds, but Class A applies when the towed vehicle is rated over ten thousand pounds and Class B when the tow is no more than that.
